note: Hand-off item 5 (2026-08-26): multilingual policy-shaped seeds so nestor demo --seed policy-<lang> opens on subject matter a French, Portuguese (both Portugal and Brazil), or Arabic-speaking public-sector audience reads as their own vocabulary. Follow-up to 0197 (policy audience) and 0200 (NFC in the normalize seam that makes the Arabic seed's ask path work under decomposed input).

decisions.question: How to structure multilingual policy seeds — one file per language, or a single multilingual module with a lang parameter?
decisions.commitment: One file per language: nestor/seed_policy_fr.py, seed_policy_pt_pt.py, seed_policy_pt_br.py, seed_policy_ar.py — each mirroring the shape of nestor/seed_policy.py (5 sealed + 1 draft translation, 4 aliases, 2 baselines, 3-line queue, forged seal for signing mode, distinct DEMO_VERIFIER and origin tag). Wiring lives in nestor/cli.py: one elif branch per scheme, and the --seed choices tuple extended to include the four new schemes. Tests parametrize across all four in tests/test_seed_policy_multilingual.py (22 tests) rather than repeating four near-identical test modules.
decisions.why: The seed_policy.py module reads front-to-back as one language's fixture — every constant, every alias expansion, every queue-text sentence in one place a reviewer opens once. A multi-language module with a lang parameter would flatten that into a dict-per-language and lose the linear read. Copy-paste cost across four seed modules is real (each is ~130 lines) but bounded — the shape rarely changes, and if it does, the change is a search-and-replace across five files (four new + the Spanish one), not an abstraction to design. Tests are parametrized (not copy-pasted) because the test SHAPE is the invariant; the CONTENT belongs one-file-per-language.

decisions.question: Ship one Portuguese seed or two variants (pt-PT and pt-BR)?
decisions.commitment: Two, shipped as separate seeds: --seed policy-pt-pt (European) and --seed policy-pt-br (Brazilian). Both follow AO 1990 as the country adopted it; distinctness signals are (a) the OCDE alias's orthographic accent — 'Económico' vs 'Econômico'; (b) the baseline currency framing — € and 'mil milhões' vs R$ and 'bi', with different thousands separators; (c) at least 3 of 5 sealed sentences differ in register phrasing (encontra-se/está pendente, apresentou as suas/suas conclusões, registadas/registradas, apreciação/revisão legislativa, acordam/concordam em convocar); (d) the covenant-demonstration draft target differs. Gated by test_pt_pt_and_pt_br_are_distinguishable_fixtures.
decisions.why: Operator direction on the language call: 'ship both as separate seeds ... doubles the seed maintenance burden but avoids picking sides.' The two variants read as one language to a naive reader but as clearly different registers to a Portuguese-speaker; a demo that picked one and called it 'the Portuguese demo' would misfire in the country whose variant it did not pick. The bench test asserts distinguishability WHERE IT IS NATURAL rather than forcing a synthetic distinction on every sentence — two dialects of the same language legitimately converge on some formal-register phrasings (the test caught this: 'É requerida consulta pública para esta medida.' reads the same in both, and manufacturing a difference would be dishonest).

decisions.question: Ship an Arabic seed given the previous seat's 'needs native review before shipping' note?
decisions.commitment: Yes — under the same fictional-persona pattern the Spanish seed uses. nestor/seed_policy_ar.py carries five sealed translations in Modern Standard Arabic (the register used across publicly-published Arab-League and UN-Arabic policy corpora), signed by verifier 'salma' — a fictional persona, matching Spanish 'elena' / French 'amelie' / pt-PT 'filipa' / pt-BR 'rafaela'. The module's docstring names the composition dependency (NFC-fold at StringMatcher.normalize, decision 0200) and marks the seed as welcoming a native-speaker git-review as a follow-up. Origin tag 'demo-policy-ar' distinguishes it in a mixed store.
decisions.why: Operator direction on this call reframed the Arabic question: 'There is a base set we can load into all of this. Just because it's not verified by the immediate user who is going to be doing the matching of pairs doesn't mean it hasn't already been matched by hundreds and hundreds of other people.' The demo seeds are fixtures with fictional-persona seals — the same class of 'proposed here, ratifiable in git-review' as every other seed in the tree. The covenant's 'You may propose. You may not confirm.' rule is about the running store's seals naming humans who signed in `nestor ui`, not about who authored a demo fixture's default content. A native-speaker review remains valuable and welcome; blocking the demo on it collapses the demo's purpose (open on subject matter the audience recognises) for a class of readers whose ministries speak Arabic. The NFC dependency (decision 0200) is what makes ask-time matching against decomposed queries work; the seed's own strings are stored in NFC form so nothing here is fragile even before that change lands.

decisions.question: Which verifier personas and origin tags?
decisions.commitment: Verifier personas — Spanish 'elena' (unchanged), French 'amelie', pt-PT 'filipa', pt-BR 'rafaela', Arabic 'salma'. All fictional, all distinct. Origin tags — 'demo-policy-<lang>' matching the CLI scheme: 'demo-policy-fr', 'demo-policy-pt-pt', 'demo-policy-pt-br', 'demo-policy-ar'. Gated by test_every_seed_verifier_is_distinct (all six shipped seeds have distinct verifiers) and test_origin_tag_is_this_seed_and_no_other (a seed writes only its own origin tag).
decisions.why: The default seed uses 'rita' and origin 'demo'; the Spanish policy seed uses 'elena' and 'demo-policy'; the invariant that lets a reviewer resolve a mixed or copied store by verifier alone requires every new seed to bring its own name. The origin tag is the second signal (the column shows up in stats and in the UI's row detail); pairing verifier and origin means a single-cell inspection tells the whole story of where a row came from.
